desc:
For the string s, count the positions i (0-indexed) such that deleting the character s[i] leaves a palindrome. Positions are counted separately even when they produce the same string. The empty string counts as a palindrome.

For example, "abca" gives 2 (delete b to get "aca" or c to get "aba"); "aaabaa" gives 4 (deleting any of the first three a or the b works); "aaaa" gives 4; "abc" gives 0.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Testing each of the n deletions costs O(n) each. Think about which deletions could possibly help.
Scan from both ends while characters match. If everything matches, the string is a palindrome; otherwise the first mismatch at l and r limits the candidate characters to s[l] and s[r].

Deleting any character of a maximal run of equal letters gives the same string, so one successful check is worth the whole run length. For a palindrome itself, only deletions inside the run of equal letters at the centre keep it a palindrome.
editorial: Case 1: s is a palindrome. Deleting position i keeps a palindrome exactly when i lies in the maximal run of equal letters that contains the centre (for even length, the two middle letters are equal and belong to the same run). Deleting anything else shifts one half against the other and breaks the symmetry. The answer is the length of that run.

Case 2: not a palindrome. Let l, r be the first mismatch. Any single deletion that works must remove a letter equal to s[l] from the run containing l, or a letter from the run containing r, because those are the only deletions that change what faces the mismatch. Test s[l+1..r] and s[l..r-1] for being palindromes; for each success add the length of the corresponding run in the whole string (all positions in a run produce the same result string). The two runs are different because s[l] != s[r].
Everything is linear: one scan, at most two palindrome checks and two run measurements. O(n) time, O(1) extra space apart from slicing.
